title: Lore Explainer: Prophecy In The World of Ice and Fire Part 1
content:
A Song of Ice and Fire and its related writings (Dunk & Egg, Fire & Blood, etc.) are stuffed to the gills with prophetic dreams and visions, almost all of which are excised completely from the TV shows, from the Old Gods visions of Bran, Jon, and Arya, through the prophecies of Melisandre and various witchy characters, to the Dragon dreams of various Targaryen characters; GRRM likes for the prophecies in his dreams to be true signposts to future events, but the prophecies are delivered mostly through metaphor and vague imagery, and often resolve in unexpected ways. As Archmaester Marwyn puts it: Prophecy will bite your prick off every time.

As the resident Song of Ice and Fire superfan, I figured, “What could be more fun than going through the prophecies and visions in the book one-by-one and explaining how they resolve or how I think they’ll resolve?” So that’s what I’m going to do; wish me luck!

This article will contain spoilers for all of the Song of Ice and Fire writings, up to and including the Winds of Winter sample chapters, Dunk & Egg, Fire and Blood, the lot. In particular, if you haven’t read the Winds of Winter sample chapters, you should go and do that first and then come back here. If you don’t want to know what happens, don’t read this article; you have been warned!

A Game of Thrones

The Direwolf

Copyright - HBO

The very first book starts out with, if not an outright prophecy, what we could call a “portent”. The Starks stumble upon a dead direwolf with 6 puppies, five grey, one white. While the kids are getting gooey-eyed over the puppies, Ned Stark looks for and locates the cause of death - the Direwolf has a foot of snapped-off antler buried in its neck. This is clearly a portent of Ned’s death at the climax of the novel; the sigil of House Stark is the direwolf, Ned has 5 trueborn children and 1 bastard, and he is killed by a Baratheon (whose sigil is the stag), either directly (if Joffrey is considered a Baratheon) or indirectly (Robert’s request leads Ned into the situation whereby he is killed).

Waking the Dragon

 “Yet that night she dreamt of one. Viserys was hitting her, hurting her. She was naked, clumsy with fear. She ran from him, but her body seemed thick and ungainly. He struck her again. She stumbled and fell. “You woke the dragon,” he screamed as he kicked her. “You woke the dragon, you woke the dragon.” Her thighs were slick with blood. She closed her eyes and whimpered. As if in answer, there was a hideous ripping sound and the crackling of some great fire. When she looked again, Viserys was gone, great columns of flame rose all around, and in the midst of them was the dragon. It turned its great head slowly. When its molten eyes found hers, she woke, shaking and covered with a fine sheen of sweat. She had never been so afraid …”

- Daenerys II, AGOT

Before her wedding, Dany dreams of being attacked by Viserys and a dragon - this is clearly a reference to Daenerys’ failed pregnancy (thighs slick with blood, hideous ripping sound) and the subsequent birth of her dragons (great columns of fire rose all around - referring to the funeral pyre of Drogo from which the dragons emerge).

Bran Stark - Credit: IrenHorrors

Bran’s Coma Dreams

At the end of Bran’s coma, just before he wakes up, he has visions as part of a broader scene where the three-eyed crow (later revealed to be Bloodraven) tries to open his third eye by making him do some impromptu parachute-free skydiving. He sees events that are currently happening elsewhere in the world, and also into the Heart of Winter, where he sees something terrifying, but it’s not articulated exactly what such a thing might be.

  “He looked east, and saw a galley racing across the waters of the Bite. He saw his mother sitting alone in a cabin, looking at a bloodstained knife on a table in front of her, as the rowers pulled at their oars and Ser Rodrik leaned across a rail, shaking and heaving. A storm was gathering ahead of them, a vast dark roaring lashed by lightning, but somehow they could not see it.”

Bran II – AGOT

Clearly refers to events occurring concurrently with Bran’s coma, at the same time Cat and Sir Rodrik are indeed taking a boat from White Harbour to King’s Landing, hoping to get to the capital before Ned. Cat is looking at the dagger with which the catspaw tried to kill Bran, and Ser Rodrik is seasick. The storm gathering ahead of them clearly refers to the turmoil that the news Cat is bringing will kick off.

“He looked south, and saw the great blue-green rush of the Trident. He saw his father pleading with the king, his face etched with grief. He saw Sansa crying herself to sleep at night, and he saw Arya watching in silence and holding her secrets hard in her heart. There were shadows all around them. One shadow was dark as ash, with the terrible face of a hound. Another was armored like the sun, golden and beautiful. Over them both loomed a giant in armor made of stone, but when he opened his visor, there was nothing inside but darkness and thick black blood.”

Bran II – AGOT

 

More events occurring at the same time as Bran’s coma, depicting Ned pleading with Robert not to kill Sansa’s direwolf, Sansa crying over the death of her Direwolf, and Arya’s guilt over the episode. Two of the shadows are easily identified; the one with “the terrible face of a Hound” is… The Hound, Sandor Clegane, easy. The second is clearly Jaime Lannister. The identity of the third (the stone giant) is much less certain; it could be Gregor Clegane, but he isn’t with the king’s party at that time. Some believe that the empty visor with thick black blood is a prophetic revelation of Gregor Clegane’s zombified existence in later books – he might be headless because Clegane’s skull is delivered to Dorne in Book 4.

 “He lifted his eyes and saw clear across the narrow sea, to the Free Cities and the green Dothraki sea and beyond, to Vaes Dothrak under its mountain, to the fabled lands of the Jade Sea, to Asshai by the Shadow, where dragons stirred beneath the sunrise.”

Bran II – AGOT

 

Almost matches the journey Daenerys will make, starting out at Pentos, going through the Dothraki Sea, to Vaes Dothrak, and then onto Qarth by the Jade Sea after Drogo’s death and the dragon’s birth. Some fans interpret this to mean that Daenerys will go to Asshai, but I would mark this one down as a failed prophecy (of which there are plenty), severed when Daenerys made the choice to go to Slaver’s Bay instead of Asshai.

Jon Snow & Ghost - Credit: IrenHorrors

Jon’s Crypt Dream

“He had never told anyone of the dream, and he did not understand why he was telling Sam now, yet somehow it felt good to talk of it. “Even the ravens are gone from the rookery, and the stables are full of bones. That always scares me. I start to run then, throwing open doors, climbing the tower three steps at a time, screaming for someone, for anyone. And then I find myself in front of the door to the crypts. It’s black inside, and I can see the steps spiraling down. Somehow I know I have to go down there, but I don’t want to. I’m afraid of what might be waiting for me. The old Kings of Winter are down there, sitting on their thrones with stone wolves at their feet and iron swords across their laps, but it’s not them I’m afraid of. I scream that I’m not a Stark, that this isn’t my place, but it’s no good, I have to go anyway, so I start down, feeling the walls as I descend, with no torch to light the way. It gets darker and darker, until I want to scream.” He stopped, frowning, embarrassed. “That’s when I always wake.” His skin cold and clammy, shivering in the darkness of his cell. Ghost would leap up beside him, his warmth as comforting as daybreak.”

Jon V - AGOT

 

Jon dreams about going down into the Winterfell crypts (which are pretty scary) - Jon’s insistence that the crypts are not “his place” while still being forced to go down into them has been taken by some fans as a hint that evidence of Jon’s true parentage was hidden by Ned in Lyanna’s grave.

The Stallion That Mounts The World

  “As swift as the wind he rides, and behind him his khalasar covers the earth, men without number, with arakhs shining in their hands like blades of razor grass. Fierce as a storm this prince will be. His enemies will tremble before him, and their wives will weep tears of blood and rend their flesh in grief. The bells in his hair will sing his coming, and the milk men in the stone tents will fear his name.” The old woman trembled and looked at Dany almost as if she were afraid. “The prince is riding, and he shall be the stallion who mounts the world.”

Danerys V - AGOT

Either interrupted by the premature birth of Dany’s stillborn deformed son, or it’s a misunderstood/symbolic oblique reference to Daenerys’ dragon Drogon.

Arya’s Dream

“When they had first come to King’s Landing, she used to have bad dreams about getting lost in the castle. Father said the Red Keep was smaller than Winterfell, but in her dreams it had been immense, an endless stone maze with walls that seemed to shift and change behind her. She would find herself wandering down gloomy halls past faded tapestries, descending endless circular stairs, darting through courtyards or over bridges, her shouts echoing unanswered. In some of the rooms the red stone walls would seem to drip blood, and nowhere could she find a window. Sometimes she would hear her father’s voice, but always from a long way off, and no matter how hard she ran after it, it would grow fainter and fainter, until it faded to nothing and Arya was alone in the dark.”

Arya III – AGOT

Arya has a somewhat trippy dream about an M.C Escher-esque Red Keep that morphs into a shifting labyrinth that goes on forever, complete with Amityville Horror-style walls dripping blood. You could argue that this whole vision foreshadows Arya’s journey through the story, getting cut off from her family, journeying through horrors, and landing at the House of Black and White in Braavos (where she is actually temporarily blinded).

Bran & Rickon’s Crypt Dreams

““I dreamed about the crow again last night. The one with three eyes. He flew into my bedchamber and told me to come with him, so I did. We went down to the crypts. Father was there, and we talked.He was sad.”

“And why was that?” Luwin peered through his tube.

“It was something to do about Jon, I think.” The dream had been deeply disturbing, more so than any of the other crow dreams..”

[...]

“You let my father be,” Rickon warned Luwin. “You let him be.”

“Rickon,” Bran said softly. “Father’s not here.”

Thoros’ Fire Vision

    “The red priest squatted down beside her. “My lady,” he said, “the Lord granted me a view of Riverrun. An island in a sea of fire, it seemed. The flames were leaping lions with long crimson claws. And how they roared! A sea of Lannisters, my lady. Riverrun will soon come under attack.”

Arya felt as though he’d punched her in the belly. “No!”

“Sweetling,” said Thoros, “the flames do not lie. Sometimes I read them wrongly, blind fool that I am. But not this time, I think. The Lannisters will soon have Riverrun under siege.””

 

This is indeed correct; shortly after the Red Wedding, the Lannisters do lay siege to Riverrun.

More False Kings

Stannis & Melisandre - Copyright HBO

    “They will not.” Melisandre’s voice was soft. “I am sorry, Your Grace. This is not an end. More false kings will soon rise to take up the crowns of those who’ve died.”

“More?” Stannis looked as though he would gladly have throttled her. “More usurpers? More traitors?”

“I have seen it in the flames.”

 

Melisandre is right; more claimants to the Iron Throne do indeed rise up in the future: Euron Greyjoy takes the throne of the Iron Islands, while Tommen sits the Iron Throne, and both “Aegon” and Daenerys are on their way.

So that's a brief rundown of the prophecies in the first three Song of Ice and Fire books and a mix of my thoughts and general fandom wisdom about what they mean. It's a long journey! Next time: A Feast For Crows, Dance With Dragons, and the various supplemental books - Dunk & Egg, Fire and Blood etc.

title: Trench Crusade Warband Focus: Black Klismos of Envy
content:
With the Court of the Seven Headed Serpent getting a massive October rules rework, Tabletop Battles is writing new subfaction focuses on each of the Sins, as they all dramatically change the way the warband plays. Perhaps the most dramatic changes are found in the Black Klismos of Envy. Envy focuses on Hell Knights, board control, positioning, and unique wargear options. Let's dig in!

The Lore

Moloch is the current Serpent Head of Envy, sitting on the Hellish council that dictates the course of the war against Creation for the Infernal forces. Jealousy and bitterness drive the forces sworn to his service, and now the upstart usurper Leviathan has been unleashed by the actions of the Scaled Saint Bartolomeo, and some of Moloch’s forces have betrayed him for a new master.

Unable to countenance any who might challenge their power, both Moloch and Leviathan spurn the more powerful lieutenants that serve the other Serpent Heads of the Court, instead relying on legions of bickering Hell Knights and serried ranks of Desecrated Saints.

Defining Traits of the Black Klismos of Envy

The first thing you’ll notice is that there are no Praetors or Sorcerers allowed in this list. Instead, we must take at least two Hell Knights and can take up to five. This can be disconcerting as, on its face, it seems like you’re losing your most powerful pieces. However, getting more access to Hell Knights allows for a lot of tactical and battlekit flexibility.

Losing access to the LEADER keyword (outside of taking a Troop Flag) can be a bit of a blow, and you’ll need to husband your resources and models carefully to make sure you aren’t taking morale checks at a significant disadvantage.

Two of your Hell Knights can also take battlekit stolen from a different warband! This opens up a few different attractive options, which we’ll cover in a bit.

We also get access to up to two Desecrated Saints! This is a huge boon as the specialized Saint aura for Envy, Maw of Comparison, is incredibly strong and allows you to lock down lanes on a battlefield exceptionally well. Desecrated Saints are powerful centerpieces in any Court warband, and getting two of them is amazing.

Uniquely, Desecrated Saints of Envy can take Iron Maiden Flails for 40 ducats, instead of the Glory cost (and limitation to Hell Knights). Their Iron Maiden Flails gain the INNATE keyword and the FIRE keyword, adding some utility to these powerful SIN marker-generating weapons. With the Saints’ NEGATE CUMBERSOME they also can be wielded without sacrificing an arm for additional weapons.

Envy’s SIN generation mechanics are a lot of fun and very characterful. At the top of every round, your Hell Knight with the lowest number of SIN markers gets a SIN marker, a sort of rolling version of Beacon of Corruption, for free. Additionally, every time one of your models with the DEMON keyword knocks down or takes out of action an enemy model, every DEMON within 6” of the DEMON who did the deed gets a SIN marker. This incentivizes you to keep your minis in small groups together so that you can piñata SIN markers whenever anything gets done.

Having two Desecrated Saints also helps with SIN generation, as Saints give any DEMON that activates within 1” of them a SIN marker (including themselves). Deploy your warband in a pair of tight groups, each around a Saint, to maximize initial SIN markers.

Additionally, we get our very own very special Glorious Deed every game, Petty Noble: the first time one of our Hell Knights gets to six SIN markers, we get a Glory. There is honestly no reason you should not be able to get this every game with some careful positioning.

Battlekit Highlights

One of the first Battlekit decisions you’ll make is what to snatch from other warbands for 2 of your Hell Knights. You have to choose a different item for each knight, so there are some interesting choices to make.

Your best bet is the Punt Gun. Its keywords fit well with a melee focused stat line that will want to be moving up the field. Hell Knights have a +0 ranged stat, so a SHOTGUN keyword with +1 DICE is attractive to make sure you hit. The ability to add BLAST is huge as well, as this synergizes extremely well with the Blood Magic Goetic spell all your Knights get for free, adding  +1 INJURY DICE to everything hit by the blast. There’s not really anything else available that has all the pieces the Punt Gun does to be a great fit for a Hell Knight of Envy.

A good melee option is an Anti-Tank Hammer. Court isn’t exactly lacking for good melee weapons, but you’re going to have a lot of Hell Knights and Saints and the AT Hammer is a great option that gets good use out of Blood Magic to one-hit KO enemies.

There are other decent choices out there, but many ranged weapons will struggle with the +0 ranged stat of the Hell Knight. I think an argument can be made for a Grenade Launcher or Satchel Charge to help even the odds against warbands with higher model counts. You could also invest in a consumable item like Martyrdom Pills to make an extremely hardy Knight, but keep in mind you’ll need to rebuy those every game in a campaign.

As for our own kit, we don’t go in for fancy laser rifles or terrain destroying lances or giant cleavers or guns shooting money here in the Black Klismos. Instead our special Battlekit is a stone knife, a barbed wire garrote, and a shield made of Fool’s Gold.

The Lying Knife is an intriguing melee weapon. It's RISKY, and gives +1 INJURY MODIFIER, but it also can borrow a keyword from any melee weapon held by an enemy you’re within 1” of. This means that you’ll need to put it on a model that can dictate who you’re going into combat with, which is why I like to put it on a Hunter of the Left Hand Path. At 12 ducats it's only two ducats more than a great hammer, for functionally the same base abilities in a one-handed package. A good deal!

The Usurper’s Saw Wire is a fun bit of kit you can use to swap out one of your normal attacks for a +2 INJURY DICE attack if the enemy model has the ELITE keyword (or is on a base the same size or bigger than yours). Put it on a Desecrated Saint and whomp on an enemy who you’ve set up for a Blood Bath attack to seal the deal. In addition, if you take the enemy out you generate two SIN markers.

Pyrite Mirror Pavaise is a difficult item to use. It’s an expensive Trench Shield at 30 ducats that lets you use a special ability of a model you’re within 1” of. With some of Envy’s movement shenanigans (specifically Coveted Position) it’s great if you can work your way into combat with something like an Observer or a War Prophet or Lieutenant, or another Court model with a cool Goetic Spell, but it's very situational for the same price as three Trench Shields.

Brand of Moloch lets you kill a friendly Wretched to power up a Goetic Spell instead of spending SIN Markers. Depending on your sin generation game and what powers you’ve unlocked for your warband this can be useful if you feel like spending Wretched instead of SIN.

Craven Vassalage is the go-to Glory item. It lets one of your Hell Knight FLY, and turn into a little bit of a Sorcerer or Praetor (depending on whether you align with Moloch or Leviathan). I’d go for the Sorcerer upgrade, as Burning Inferno is a great spell.

The Magic of Charlatans

Coveted Position

Our number one spell. Coveted Position lets you swap models’ physical positions on the battlefield for two SIN (within 12”). If you’ve ever played any MOBA ever you know this is the most bonkers ability for a pick. You can put your Hell Knight where you want them to set up Punt Gun shots or long range charges, and stick an enemy right where you want them. There’s also no restriction on yeeting yourself or an enemy model straight into combat range.

Meat Shield

If there’s one thing Envy loves doing, it's killing Wretched. Stick 'em in an Iron Maiden, kill them to cast a spell, or, with Meat Shield, make them take a hit for you.

What’s Yours Is Mine

Another very situational spell. If you’re playing against someone who generates a lot of BLESSING Markers it might be nice, or if you're playing another Court player you can zero-sum away some SIN. I’m not a huge fan of this spell.

Playing the Warband

We've found Envy lists to be fairly tall. Focus on getting a few Hell Knights, definitely take both Saints right off the rip, then fill in with a Hunter of the Left Hand Path and Pit Locusts.

For your Hell Knights, lean into what they’re good at. Give them a decent melee weapon like an Anti-Tank Hammer or a Hellblade (save your Malebranche Sword for a Saint) and give them ranged weapons that won’t penalize them for shooting as well as a half-blind New Antioch conscript, like a Punt Gun or Ophidian Rifle.

Your Saints are your big heavy hitters. Give one of them the Malebranche Sword and the other a Iron Maiden Flail to whale on your enemies. If you can afford to sacrifice a Wretched when you run into a heavily armored list, cram one into the flail to ignore armor and generate SIN. With their charge limiting aura, I also recommend taking a Tormentor Chain on a Saint to dictate the pace of the battle and positioning of enemy units.

You don’t have a LEADER and your Elites don’t have TOUGH, so be careful with your Hell Knights. They get an INNATE, IMPERVIOUS -2 armor stat which is great, but they’re still vulnerable to a random bolt action rifle shot, so pick your engagements and don’t rush in.

Keep your forces in small groups within 6” of each other so that any time one model knocks an enemy down or takes them out, you give multiple models SIN.  With decent positioning and play you should end up with more than enough SIN throughout the game.

In objective based missions you’ll suffer from the same problems as other Court warbands, getting out activated and out captured by the enemy, so you need to focus on killing enemies to force them off objectives and hopefully break their morale. Bully enemy models and don’t let yourself get spread thin. Envy has a lot of tools to dictate positioning, and it's our strength.

Sample List

800 Ducat, 6 Glory

Elites 

Hell Knight - 131D

Upgrades & Choices: Corpse Candles

Battlekit: Punt Gun, Trench Club, Trench Club, Infernal Iron Armour

Hell Knight - 153D

Upgrades & Choices: Corpse Candles, Coveted Position

Battlekit: Anti-Tank Hammer, Infernal Iron Armour, Trench Club

Troops 

Desecrated Saint - 178D | 3G

Battlekit: Tormentor Chain, Malebranche Sword, Trench Club

Desecrated Saint - 158D | 3G

Battlekit: Tormentor Chain, Hellblade, Trench Club

Pit Locust - 90D

Battlekit: Reinforced Armour

Pit Locust - 90D

Battlekit: Reinforced Armour

Final Thoughts

Playing Envy is a huge departure from how most Court lists will play. Your list will be incredibly brittle, with limited TOUGH, no LEADER, and expensive mid tier elites that will do all your heavy lifting. But the list is very strong, focusing on board control and tools that are hard for your opponent to anticipate. Envy has one of the trickier SIN marker generation mechanics, but by exploiting your positioning and wargear advantages they can generate more SIN than they can reasonably spend. Envy is one of the most characterful and fun subfactions to play, especially when you lean into your theme.

And remember, when in doubt, if you’re losing, it’s clearly the fault of how underpowered and unfair your warband is in comparison to everyone else, who gets cooler toys and models than you ever will. Complain about this loudly and at length, as Moloch would want you to.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Ghosts of Cadia, by Rob Young
content:
Image credit: Games Workshop

This year sure seems to be shaping up to the the "year of the surprise return," isn't it? Just this week we saw the mothership announce that Vorx and the boys are coming back in a sequel to Chris Wraight's 2018 masterpiece The Lords of Silence (review). While we don't have a release date for Realm of Silence just yet, it's pa pretty safe bet that we won't have long to wait given the relatively quick turnarounds we're seeing between teaser and preorder.

Then last July came the news that Orikan the Diviner and Trazyn the Infinite- everyone's favorite Warhammer frenemies from Robert Rath's The Infinite and the Divine (review)- would have a return engagement in The Wicked and the Warped (review).

And just the month before, we'd already seen another return: Darya Nevic, hero of 2023's Longshot. If the plucky Cadian Sniper's return seemed a little less heralded or portentous, don't blame author Rob Young. The Lords of Silence is a Black Library Readers' Hall of Fame-winning book, while The Infinite and the Divine is one of the Black Library's runaway hits, famously dethroning Dan Abnett's Horus Rising as the 'top book' at Warhammer World last November.

Longshot, meanwhile, was a softcover-only release that was part of the long-running Astra Militarum series that has recently included William Crowe's Veterans of the Fall (review) and Final Deployment by R S Wilt (review). These have tended to be one-off affairs, with only Andy Clark's Steel Tread getting the sequel treatment with 2025's Demolisher (review).

Still, the sniper-versus-sniper dynamic often likened to a 40K version of the Jude Law and Ed Harris film Enemy at the Gates made Longshot a standout entry. Given a chance to bring her back, could Young recapture some of the magic that made his debut novel such a success?

The Story

Ghosts of Cadia sees Sergeant Nevic and her Cadian 217th sharpshooter team on Parrescum, an Imperial world in the midst of a bloody civil war. So bloody, in fact, that they've gone from deployment to deployment, mission to mission without rest or respite- and it's beginning to take its toll. With an unnatural storm protecting the rebel-occupied capital from orbital strike, it's up to the Cadian soldiers and their elite Kasrkin strike teams to root out the rot the hard way.

Stretched to the absolute limit, Nevic is rocked when a chance encounter on the battlefield appears to be a ghost from her past. Tasked with an assassination strike that could help end the siege with a shot, her mission puts her on a collision course between the echo of her past and the future of the war.

Image credit: Games Workshop

Scoping the Snipers

It would have been easy for Young to lean into another sniper-centered war story. After all, that's literally their job. But while long-range marksmanship certainly has its place here, I give him a lot of credit for trying something different. While the battles on the ground are critical to the tale, it's the battles inside that give the book much of its weight.

Through Ghosts of Cadia, Young looks to explore what it means to a soldier when the demands on a soldier eclipse the needs of the human. This is fertile ground for storytelling, mined by fiction ranging from Catch-22 by Joseph Heller to Dan Abnett's Only in Death. With her team taking mission after mission with little hope of respite, Young does the work of establishing the effects of this on Darya's decision-making and leadership.

Adroitly, Young waits until later in the story to draw a line under it, with Darya finally being called out by a Kasrkin sergeant. It's terrific show-don't-tell storytelling, and brings a welcome level of real-world grittiness to the table.

"We all get the dreams, Nevic. The thing is, we're all combat-fatigued to some degree. The human mind isn't made to process the kind of loss and trauma that we experience, so you find ways to deal with it. I see my people just like you see yours, and there are nights it really scares me. If they ever catch me I'll let you know what they're about."

"So how do you get around it? How do you compartmentalize it?"

"Training. Mental exercises, things like that," Tystas said. "One of the key ones we get taught in the Kasrkin is objective setting - you break down a job into its smallest parts and complete each of them in turn until the objective is met. Each part feels small and achievable, rather than one big impossible task. I might have one that'll help clear your head for a few days, if you want?"

"Go on then, explain it to me," Darya said.

Unfortunately, though its refreshing to see that level of realism it's not quite enough to carry the book on its own, and while Young commendably aimed high here it was a bit of an uneven result.

For one thing, I was about a third of the way through the book when it occurred to me that I still really didn't know a lot about the characters. After all, it had been awhile since I'd read Longshot, but Ghosts didn't spend a lot of time rebuilding those connections and relationships for the reader. Sequel-writing isn't just about crafting a good second story; one essential ingredient is building a bridge from the first book to the second.

Consider how Abnett approached this problem in the Eisenhorn trilogy. There's a 98-year gap between Xenos and Malleus, but a read of the early annotations in the latter title's Illustrated and Annotated Edition shows how important maintaining familiarity with the characters- the "narrative catch-up"- was for him as a writer. Note too that both these books were published less than six months apart in 2001, when a contemporary reader might well have the memories of the first book still relatively top of mind.

That only makes the case that much stronger for a sequel published three years later. While Young does often refer back to the events of Longshot, in the main these were "brand new" characters for me as I began the sequel, and they remained that way throughout. An opportunity missed.

Another place the book might have benefitted a bit more from editor's guidance was in its climax. I won't spoil it here, of course, but after an extensive build-up to the end of the story, it all resolves fairly quickly and simply- almost to the point of an anticlimax. I'd have preferred to see a slower burn, perhaps using alternating point-of-view switches to help ratchet up tension before the final moment. After all, we've been waiting the entire book for that moment, it should have a payoff commensurate with its import.

That's a shame, because the interpersonal character dynamics really start to gel as the book rounds third, landing some very satisfying emotional beats.

Image credit: Cubicle 7

Final Thoughts

Interestingly enough, here's what I said about Young's Master of Rites in my review this past February:

Overall, when I note the book being uneven, it's because Young showed so many good ideas but didn't quite carry them as through as I'd have hoped. 

Unfortunately, the same applies here with Ghosts of Cadia. From Darya's engagement with the Kasrkin to the mystery of a hidden reliquary, there's a lot of great material here. And just as with Master of Rites, Young gives us an absolutely riveting middle act that shows the kinds of tableaus he's capable of envisioning. In the previous book it was the weirdness of a mist-enshrouded planet having returned from the warp, and here it's a sinister chaos storm sequence that's bursting with suspense and body horror. Scintillating stuff that leaves you wanting so much more.

While Ghosts of Cadia never quite equals the sum of its parts, but it doesn't entirely miss, either. Even if it didn't manage to be the book it feels like it could have been, there's still a lot to enjoy with Darya Nevic and her sharpshooters.

title: Pokémon accidentally reveals future cards from next year's McDonalds collab
content:
In a now-deleted post intended to promote the McDonald's Pokémon cards launching in a cross-promotion on November 10, the Pokémon Company has accidentally shared details of next year's collab instead. This revealed cards that were not supposed to be shown yet, perhaps not until this time in 2027. These cards, posted by Pokebeach, have a 2027 copyright date on the bottom and an M27 stamp, making their identity clear.

Sadly (or, depending on your outlook on leaks, happily) there aren't any Gen 10 Pokémon in the collection. McDonald's partnerships typically use old reprints, not new cards, so the vast majority of these are simply repeats from the past couple of years, with art and effects we've seen before. Yawn! Not all of them though.

The lone exception is a squirtle card that is mechanically unique and has new artwork by illustrator Kariya. This simple squirtle has an attack called Splatter, which deals 10 HP damage to an opponent's benched Pokémon.

Since we're not looking too far into the future here, we can assume that this card will be coming out pretty soon - perhaps Japan's first 2027 Pokémon set, Mega x Mega Parade. Fans are treating this as a strong sign that Mega Blastoise will be getting a card soon - why else would there be a new Squirtle?

The actual 2026 McDonalds promo cards include Palafin, Chandelure, and Tyranitar. For the very first time, these Pokémon promo cards will be accompanied by toys! Remember toys?

There'll be two cards and one toy in each Pokémon Happy Meal, from a possible selection of 15 plastic figurines.

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Melee Attack Sequence Guide
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m going through a step by step example for a melee attack with a unit from start to finish!

Eligible to Use Normal Fight

While the eligibility for Normal Fight is simply “your unit is engaged,” the unit has to be eligible to fight in the first place to get to this point; to be eligible to fight a unit must be:

  • engaged now,
  • engaged at the start of the fight step (12.04)
  • or have made a charge move this turn.

Eligible to Use Overrun Fight

To use the Overrun Fight type, your unit needs to meet one of the latter two criteria or have become engaged during the step; this can happen in a few different ways.

Selecting a Melee Weapon

Unlike ranged attacks, when selecting weapons to use from your unit, models can only make melee attacks with one weapon each.

You must select one melee weapon that model has.

Models without melee weapons cannot make melee attacks at all; there’s no universal close combat weapon in 11th like some older editions have had.

Selecting Targets

Selecting targets is all about engagement range; a model in the target unit must be within engagement range of the model with the weapon being targeted.

Unlike ranged weapons, melee weapons can select one or more targets per weapon up to the A characteristic of that weapon. So if a weapon has an A of 2, it can select two different enemy units for that weapon if both of those enemy units have a model within engagement range of this attacking model.

There are exceptions to the one weapon rule, though; the EXTRA ATTACKS special rule allows models to also make melee attacks with any and all weapons with this ability.

Each time a unit containing one or more models with an [EXTRA ATTACKS] weapon fights, those models will make attacks with those weapons in addition to any others. In the Select Weapons step (04.01), for each of those models, you must select:

    • All of that model’s [EXTRA ATTACKS] weapons.
    • One of that model’s other melee weapons, if possible.

Resolving Attacks

Attack Die Groups (Identical Attacks)

Now we’ve figured out our targets, we need to resolve attacks; these happen in groups of identical attacks vs each enemy unit we’ve targeted.

Identical attacks are those that have the same BS/WS, S, AP and D characteristics, and which are affected by the same applicable abilities and rules.

This will come up more frequently if the attacking unit has several models, some of which are armed with different melee weapons but it does still occur in the Carnifex example as identical attacks are per target. So when we resolve them we should do them in groups per target unit.

The Attack Sequence

The fighting player will choose which order to resolve their weapons in and run through the Attack Sequence [05] for each weapon that has targeted the chosen enemy unit.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!

title: Celebrate Warhammer day with up to 93% off its best licensed videogames
content:
October 29's Warhammer day celebrates the world's biggest wargame with exclusive minis, fresh hordes of merch, and deals, deals, deals. Some of Warhammer's top videogames are on sale for a limited time on platforms like Fantatical. And the discounts are deep, with some games as much as 80% off. You might want to act swiftly, though - the sale only lasts until November 1.

Fanatical has a broad range of games and DLC on sale, though it takes some digging to find high discounts (on games that are actually good). Thankfully, many of the top titles from our Warhammer 40k games guide are going cheap.

The steepest discount goes to Warhammer : The End Times - Vermintide. Fatshark's 2015 co-op action game is a delightfully chaotic mess of shooting, melee, and Skaven. Both the base game and collector's edition are 93% off, so you can pick this one up for as low as $2.24 (£1.72). Or, if you want extra cosmetics and goodies, deluxifying will cost just $3.37 (£2.54).

Vermintide 2, the hit shooter's sequel, is just as well-loved by Warhammer fans. And, lucky for those who'd like a more modern take on the genre, it's just as cheap. Fanatical offers an 85% discount, taking the price down to $4.49 (£3.56).

Plus, the spiritual successor to these games is on sale. Darktide takes the aggressive horde-slaying to the 40k universe, dropping you into the Chaos-riddled hive city of Tertium. The fine-tuned gameplay of Vermintide is just as engrossing (and visually gnarly) in the 41st millennium At 75% off, the game is now just $9.99 (£8.24).

Beyond the realms of first-person action shooters, we have games like Warhammer 40k: Battlesector. This turn-based strategy game is as close as a videogame gets to the feel of pushing your armies around on tabletop. We had our issues with the rather routine gameplay loop at launch (learn more in our review), but updates have helped trim the fat and shave down the game's rough edges. If you want to form your own opinion, now's the time to experiment - at 76% off, Battlesector sets you back just $9.59 (£8.42).

Sticking with turn-based strategy games, Chaos Gate Daemonhunters is also 77% off. The XCOM-like gives you a Grey Knights unit to specialize (and keep alive) as they battle the forces of Nurgle. It's a challenging, satisfying tactical experience that's a must-have for lovers of both Warhammer and XCOM. You can learn more in our full review - or you can spend $12.64 (£10.34) and find out for yourself.

Now, for something a little more out-there. Shootas, Blood & Teef is a silly, slapstick side-scroller where Orks do what they do best - wreck everything in sight. Its campaign mode is only four hours long, but what it lacks in length it makes up for in gleeful fun. Fanatical offers only a 25% discount on this one, but it still only costs $14.97 (£12.35). If you're after something quirky, this might be your bag.

Another unusual one is the 20% discount offered for Dawn of War 4, a game that isn't even out yet. The brand-new real-time strategy game drops on December 3, so we can't say for sure how good it is, but as part of an established series, there's plenty of hype around its launch. If you want to get in on the ground floor, Fanatical's discount lets you pre-order for $47.99 (£39.99).

'But wait!', I hear you cry. 'If this is a sale of the best games, where the hell is Space Marine 2?!' It's there, aggravated reader. The discount just isn't that great. Fanatical offers just 12% off our favorite-ever Warhammer game. $52.79 (£48.39) is better than no discount at all, but you might find it cheaper by shopping around.

That's all for now! Want to chat more about Warhammer in general? We're always open to wargaming discussion in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Pokémon TCG reveals sharp new Rayquaza box with Delta Reign's missing full art
content:
The Pokémon Company has announced a new Delta Reign-adjacent product: the Mega Rayquaza ex Premium Tournament Collection. Housed in a swish green-and-gold box, this collection has eight booster packs, plus Mega Rayquaza accessories like sleeves and a deck box. The product is launching on February 12, 2027.

We expected to see it pretty soon, and indeed this is where the Rayquaza ultra rare full art card from the Japanese set, which will not be found in English-language booster packs, appears - as a promo that's included with every box. The collection also has a few other promo cards worth a quick mention: foil versions of Zinnia's Trust, Adventure Lantern, and Mega Rayquaza Cap, plus the split cards that form Legendary Summit Stadium.

Compared to 2025's Iono and Lillie Premium Tournament Collections, this box has a couple of extra packs - neat! However, the pricing has not been confirmed yet: it's plausible that it's been bumped up to match. According to product shots, there are four Delta Reign packs, four Pitch Black packs inside.

Another notable difference is that (fittingly given Rayquaza's typing), TPC has used Dragon Shield for the deck box and sleeves this time, instead of Ultra Pro. We'll have to see if that's a one off, or if Pokémon has changed partners for good!

Gotta say, the accessories look particularly great here. I would love to have that deck box, and the sleeves are nice too (though that text at the bottom kind of spoils them for me).

Are you going to try and get hold of one of these in February? How heavily scalped do you think they will be? Come join the conversation over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: How a wargaming beginner fell in love with Trench Crusade
content:
Most people I meet get into tabletop games through friends. There's the college buddy that introduces the intricacies of a euro, or the cousin who patiently explains the keywords on a trading card. Heck, sometimes you're lucky enough to have a gaming parent show you the ropes from a young age.

When your gateway into gaming is a person, it offers many perks. You're more open to trying something new, because the company is pleasant. Perhaps more importantly, you're not afraid to suck. Tabletop games can feel like an alien language to a complete beginner, and fear of scoffs or judgement are natural. The trustworthiness of a table can make or break someone's relationship with the whole hobby.

All this is to say: I never got into miniature wargaming. No one ever darkened my door with a Warhammer 40k starter set, eager to show me a sprue. I visited wargaming groups a few times, but, despite my curiosity, I never found the courage to join a table. I've been condescended by unfamiliar playmates in the past, and it's an experience I've never been keen to repeat.

What, then, would it take for me to overcome these barriers - and venture into a new hobby alone?

Approachability is number one. I love a 12-hour board game as much as the next nerd, but I wouldn't force one on a beginner. Easily remembered rules ward against embarrassment, and they make it simple to jump into the fray.

Next, the game needs to do something truly enticing. This factor is a little more personal, as we all have different tastes. Me? I'm interested in narrative experiences. I prefer horror over levity, and I lean towards myth and fantasy over technology and space suits.

I'm also a huge sucker for a strong art selection. If I want to stare at a rulebook as much as I want to play it, you've found a way to get the game in my hands - and after that, I'm more likely to start playing.

Enter Trench Crusade. This WW1 skirmish game, set on an alternate Earth where demons have plagued the planet since the Crusades, is an up-and-comer on the wargaming scene. It's got nowhere near the brand power and player support of Warhammer 40k. I'm told, however, it relives wargaming's golden years, by means of scrappy satanic minis.

All this sounds like catnip to the grognard, and it probably is. Fellow writer Tim Linward adores it, and he's got the 10/10 Carcass Front review to prove it. The attraction is evident for existing wargamers. What might be less obvious is how appealing Trench Crusade is to the novice.

Factor one: approachability. The basic rules of Trench Crusade can be explained in less than 10 pages. In fact, that Carcass Front box only needs three. A slim, sturdy summary booklet covers the essentials, with a handful of extra keywords explained on the warband sheets.

At an Essen Spiel demo, my kindly teacher walked us through the rules in about 10 minutes. If it weren't for the eager nervousness of two beginner players, he probably could have explained even faster. These are your dice, and these are your infantry. Here is a measuring tape - time to take your turn.

It's important not to mistake simplicity for a lack of complexity. As I mused with designer Tuomas Pirinen later, the word 'simple' doesn't do Trench Crusade justice. The rules might be learned in minutes, but mastering them is a far longer pursuit. In fact, what makes the game so enticing is how many decisions it offers with so few rules.

There's my second buzzword, 'enticing'. The wealth of tactical choices in Trench Crusade gripped me after just a few turns. You can move every turn, but how will you do it? Will you Charge to trigger a melee assault, retreat out of an enemy's reach, or reposition for a better shot at range?

And then, there's the Dash action. This separate, second bout of movement is a Risky action, meaning you roll to see whether it's even possible. Fail, and your turn is over, whatever plans are left unfulfilled. That's how I ended up with a Drowned Chorister who stood stock still for three whole turns.

Each time, I chose to start with a Risky Dash instead of my guaranteed Move action. That way, I could line up a successful charge against the enemy without spending a turn in a vulnerable spot - unless, of course, I rolled badly. Which I did. Twice.

Every roll in Trench Crusade is a 2D6 roll. You can gain 'advantage' or 'disadvantage', which adds or subtracts D6s from the pool. However many you roll, though, you take the two best or worst results. Generally, you want a seven or above to succeed.

Did I make sound strategic choices with that Chorister? Definitely not, but making those mistakes was a hoot. Quickly, I could assess my failings' impact on the board and learn lessons. Trench Crusade's snappy turns create this wonderful space where mistakes don't feel punishing - they're thrilling. I might be on the backfoot this turn, but I'm already eager to tip the scales on the next.

Let's talk about that Chorister a little more. Mechanically, they have nothing to offer as ranged attackers, but they're a menace in melee. The menace is made worse by their Unholy Hymns ability, which gives enemy models -1 dice to Success Rolls if they're within eight inches of your Chorister. Attacking, dashing, and escaping all become more perilous.

Trench Crusade transforms its landscape with these small details. A Stigmatic Nun might see a Chorister on the horizon and decide to chuck a grenade from the safety of cover - because its 'Ignore Long Range' keyword allows her to attack without penalty. Or maybe that player's Leper Pilgrim advances anyway, because their Flamethrower guarantees an automatic hit.

Each decision, however carefully calculated, comes down to the dice, who might not always favor you. From that tense space between luck and tactics, a story appeared. I first noticed it when my opponent began gleefully narrating his warband's moves. He wasn't moving plastic around a map; he was peeking around corners, stomping through tough terrain, or stumbling off edges.

I don't have much wargaming experience to compare with. Maybe this is par for the course. But, as a lover of roleplay and emergent storytelling, it made my starter scenario special. Trench Crusade got its hooks in me, and already it was dragging me down to Leviathan's lair.

And that's just the storytelling side of the rules. Trench Crusade has a dedicated setting, and it's stuffed to bursting with moreish lore. Those Drowned Choristers? Zealous humans who drowned themselves to serve the forces of Hell. Stigmatic Nuns? Brutal women who mutilate themselves into ecstasy, then dominate the battlefield with firearms and throwing crucifixes.

That's just the tip of the corpse-strewn iceberg. Trench Crusade has centuries of horrific history, starting with the opening of Jerusalem's hellgate in The Crusades, and reaching us 800 years later, from the trenches of No Man's Land. It's a vivid, incredibly well-researched Catholic apocalypse, with the teachings of Christ taken to gruesome extremes.

In a word: gnarly. In a few more words: I feel like I've been Raptured. Trench Crusade's dark, thoughtful writing, combined with the stunning visuals spearheaded by Mike Franchina, swept me off my feet to someplace sacred (yet delightfully desecrated). The sights I've seen are sublime in the truest sense of the word - awe-inspiring to the point of terror.

I may be a wargaming beginner, but I'm ready to prostrate myself in worship at Trench Crusade's altar. It has that holy trinity I talked about: sick art, enticing storyelling, and rules that scream elegance. After one demo, I'm officially a convert. Now, I just need to figure out how to build these Carcass Front miniatures…

You can learn a bit more about Trench Crusade's sublime stories in Tim's piece on the lore, or my latest interview with Tuomas Pirinen. If you'd like to give me your best painting tips, you should swing by the Wargamer Discord, too - we're slowly building a wholesome little wargaming community over there.

title: To our horror, this Warhammer mini is completely edible
content:
Connor, who runs the Instagram account Crypsis Art, specializes in painting miniatures to terrify and disturb, and now this Canadian artist is creating a Warhammer work that you could actually physically eat… though that doesn't mean anyone not already in the service of Nurgle would want to...

Produced as a proof of concept for the horror and grimdark miniature painting contest Horrors of the Flesh, Connor's Age of Sigmar Lord of Plagues mini is constructed from gelatin - and has an astonishing level of detail. It's basically Warhammer's version of 'is this cake'?

Created from ballistic gelatine, cast in a silicone mold, the miniature has bones of pasta, and was painted to perfection with corn starch slurry. It does not look or sound appetizing, nor is it meant to, but you could eat it. Crypsis says they also experimented with a version that had hot sauce for blood, which I can't imagine made it tastier…

"Painting on gelatine is quite the challenge," he adds. "So sloppy impasto is the only technique available on a budget."

"My art is a reflection of what inspires and disgusts me the most, with a heavy dose of body horror and a little bit of science," the creator says. "I started with body horror, making lots of David Cronenberg-inspired minis, then leaned into a bit of science with things like tensegrity warhammer minis. My wobbly Nurgle mini is the confluence of those two things: visceral body horror to disgust and a little bit of science to provide some novelty."

While this Lord of Plagues is made from consumable ingredients, it won't be safely eatable for long.

"In my mind, the natural next step for this is going beyond body horror and leaning into actual rot. With a mold that can cast various organic materials, I plan on making something that can either be inoculated with fungus or just decompose into something really gross."

"For my other minis, I'm finally moving past Cronenberg and planning on making stuff inspired by John Carpenter and Guillermo del Toro".

You can share your favorite minis and get inspiration from our community, over on the Wargamer Discord. And don't forget to check out Crypsis Art's other work!

title: Top 10 new spells in the D&D World of Warcraft book
content:
The new D&D World of Warcraft book is available in early access from November 3, and the spoilers are coming thick and fast. Spoilers is definitely more of an MTG term, but when influencers are spilling secret spells and stat blocks from the new book, I'm not sure what else to call it. Either way, the skinny is this: we've seen pretty much every spell in D&D Wow, and I have opinions.

These new spell reveals come courtesy of the YouTube channel Insight Check, who shared a deep dive into the book's new spells earlier this week. They provide the rules text, but the analysis below is all mine.

Before I tell you about my favorite spells, though, an important note. Many of these spells are specific to the DnD classes available in the World of Warcraft book. Basically, you'll need to check with your DM before adding them to a standard D&D build. Should they be available for all D&D builds? Only time and more testing will tell…

Wrath

LevelCantrip
Spell listDruid
Casting timeAction
Range60 feet
ComponentsV, S
DurationInstantaneous

I love a good cantrip, and Wrath certainly fits the bill. You make a ranged spell attack against a target, dealing 1d8 Lightning damage on a hit. Plus, a successful hit reduces their Speed by 10 feet until the end of your next turn. Wrath scales much like other cantrips, upping to 2d8 damage at level five, 3d8 at level 11, and 4d8 at level 17.

That speed debuff feels like a fitting addition to the Control-driven Druid's repertoire. For me, it's up there with the likes of Shocking Grasp, a cantrip that combines damage and battle utility. Is it the best cantrip ever designed? Probably not. Will I be using it a lot as a Druid player? Oh yes.

Throw Glaive

LevelOne
Spell listRanger (Demon Hunter only)
Casting timeAction
Range60 feet
ComponentsV, S
DurationInstantaneous

Throw Glaive is a ranged spell attack that, when it hits a creature or object, deals 1d8 slashing and 1d8 fire damage. The magical glaive then bounces to a different target of your choice within 30 feet, and you make a new attack and damage roll for the second target.

Throw Glaive can be upcast toad 1d8 fire damage for each extra spell level. Plus, the glaive ricochets up to a number of times equal to the spell slot extended. If you can guarantee hits with reasonable consistency, that's a lot of potential attacks. This spell is cheap, flavorful, and a lot of fun.

Moonfire

LevelOne
Spell listDruid
Casting timeBonus Action
Range60 feet
ComponentsV
DurationOne round

Moonfire's target makes a Dexterity save, taking 2d8 Radiant damage on a failure. A failed save also causes them to shed dim light in a 10-foot radius, preventing them from having the Invisible condition until the end of their next turn. Plus, at the end of their next turn, they take an extra 1d8 Radiant damage.

Successful saves still deal half damage, and the initial and later damage both increase by 1d8 for each spell slot above level one. 3d8 damage isn't too shabby at level one, and Moonfire provides several methods for disrupting the schemes of magical enemies. I'd call that pretty good value for money.

Guided Prayer

LevelThree
Spell listPaladin
Casting timeReaction, which you take when you become Bloodied or take damage while you are Bloodied
RangeSelf
ComponentsV
DurationInstantaneous

Guided Prayer restores 8d4 + your spellcasting ability modifier in HP. It also gives you advantage on your next attack roll before the end of your next turn. Advantage isn't too tough to come by in 5.5e, but if you're in a dire spot, gaining it along with some healing feels pretty sweet.

Traditionally, D&D players prefer to kill enemies (they say it's the best form of healing). A Paladin with limited spell slots may find Smites more generally applicable, but I still think this spell has its uses in specific circumstances.

Chaos Nova

LevelFour
Spell listRanger (Demon Hunter only)
Casting timeAction
RangeSelf
ComponentsV
DurationInstantaneous

Chaos Nova creates a 20-foot emanation of chaos energy around you, dealing 2d6 Force damage to each creature of your choice in range. Those same targets also make a Wisdom save, becoming Stunned until the end of your next turn on a fail.

A mass stun is, frankly, ridiculous. Throw yourself into a horde of enemies, and you have the power to completely upend the encounter's action economy. Yes, you have to contend with the game's most common saving throw, but a few unlucky rolls could help you seriously ruin your DM's day. I'm glad this is so class-specific, because I think it's incredibly easy to abuse.

Divine Shield

LevelFour
Spell listPaladin
Casting timeReaction, which you take when you take damage
RangeSelf
ComponentsV
DurationOne round

I'm just gonna quote D&D directly here, because the rules text does a great job of explaining how powerful this is. "You have immunity to all damage until the start of your next turn, including the triggering damage." Then there's a little explainer saying your Speed can't be reduced for the duration either, but wow. Immune to all damage. Period.

A level-four spell slot is expensive, but Divine Shield is Shield with guaranteed results. Saving that fourth-level spell slot could literally save your character's life.

This is only available to Paladins, something I have mixed feelings about. I love seeing class-exclusive spells, because 5.5e makes it increasingly challenging to give each class a distinct identity. However, the Paladin has had a lot of top-tier new subclasses and features in the last year or two. I'm happy for Paladins, but I'm also concerned the class might get a little too good if this keeps up…

Starfall

LevelFour
Spell listDruid
Casting timeAction
Range120 feet
ComponentsV, S, M
DurationOne round

Man, World of Warcraft has been really good to Druids. Starfall summons a 30-foot-radius, 40-foot-high cylinder that forces those inside to make a Dexterity saving throw. It doles out 7d8 damage on a failure, and half damage on a success. Until the start of your next turn, any creature that enters the space or ends its turn there takes Radiant damage equal to your Druid level (but only once per turn).

Imagine Moonbeam, but also huge. It hangs around for significantly less time, but what it lacks in staying power it makes up for with a tasty amount of damage. A level-four Moonbeam offers 4d10 Radiant damage, in comparison. If you can hit a creature with both the initial and later damage, that's an average of 35.5 knocked off the enemy's HP. Not too shabby!

Holy Nova

LevelFour
Spell listCleric
Casting timeAction
RangeSelf
ComponentsV
DurationInstantaneous

A 30 foot emanation surrounds you, with effects on both friend and foe. Holy Nova forces enemies to make a Constitution save, taking 5d6 Radiant damage on a fail or half as much on a success. Meanwhile, allies regain 3d6 HP. Cast at a higher level, and the damage and healing both increase by 1d6 for each additional spell slot level.

A lot of the spells and abilities in this book have the power to both harm and heal. It certainly saves you a lot of time. Holy Nova might be the best example of this design philosophy. If you're in close quarters, you could afflict or affect everyone on the field - which feels pretty great.

Innervate

LevelFive
Spell listDruid
Casting timeAction
Range30 feet
ComponentsV
DurationInstantaneous

Innervate gives a creature of your choice within range a level-four spell slot. That's it. The slot lasts until the target's next long rest, and it can use the spell slot to cast any spell it has prepared. Oh, and because you're a Druid, Innervate also gives you back an expended use of Wild Shape.

Trading a level-five spell slot for a level-four one is a bit of a downgrade. In many cases, it's simply a better value proposition to cast your level-five spell. However, I can see plenty of circumstances where Innervate would be welcome. Perhaps, for example,a Moon Druid wants to focus more on its beast forms, and they're willing to trade a spell slot so the party Wizard can give them Haste.

Innervate is for those times when a party's dwindling resources need a reshuffle to ensure optimal turns. It might not be a must-have for every Druid, but there's plenty of reason to consider it for future spell lists.

Apotheosis

LevelNine
Spell listCleric
Casting timeBonus action
RangeSelf
ComponentsV
DurationOne minute

You take on an angelic form that gives you a Fly speed of 90 feet for the duration, plus resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, radiant, and slashing damage. Additionally, whenever you cast a spell using a spell slot that restores HP or radiant damage, you resolve the effects as if you'd used a spell slot two levels higher than the one actually used (max level is nine).

Yes, this is as high-level as it gets with spell slots - but you get fantastic maneuverability, you're tough to hit, and your spells are far more potent. There's no expensive material component, and there's no need to concentrate. This is the Cleric in their most nova form. Apotheosis might be the new must-have for high-level characters of that class.

Want to hear more about D&D World of Warcraft? We'll have a full review to share in just a few days, so watch this space. You can stay up-to-date with our coverage in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you want to start preparing for your next character builds, why not check out our guides to DnD classes and DnD races?

title: MTG Star Trek made the impossible - a counterspell that's fun for both sides
content:
Nothing stings more than having a great spell countered - except stax, extra turn spells, mass land destruction, and targeted discard; Magic: The Gathering has a lot of dirty tricks. But the new Star Trek set has done the unthinkable. It's produced a counterspell that's fun for everyone at the table. Oh, and also, it's red.

Brazen Bluff is a two mana red instant that offers your opponent a dilemma. Either they exile their unresolved spell while it's on the stack, or you get to cast any noncreature spell you like from your hand for free. The question is, what have you got in your hand? Does your opponent feel lucky?

This is a fantastic reference to the Star Trek: The Original Series episode The Corbomite Maneuver, where Captain Kirk is able to bluff his way out of a battle by pretending the Enterprise has a secret weapon on board - when actually they were just doomed.

This card is great flavor then, as it creates the same Poker-style problem for your opponent to chew on. Does the Brazen Bluff player genuinely have something apocalyptic, or are they making things up? You can only cast (and target) non-creature spells with Brazen Bluff. If you choose to run it, maybe you put Worldfire in your deck just for fun.

It's worth noting that in Magic, you are able to show hidden information to your opponent (as long as it's hidden information you have access to). So you could remove the mystery and simply show your opponent the card you plan to play, to try and strongarm them into going the way you want. There's even an opportunity for politicking here. "Let me cast this for free, and I promise not to use it on you".

If you want to be a spoilsport, you can point out that this is simply a worse version of Negate, and it's useless if you have no other cards in hand. But the point is that it's a worse Negate in mono red, which traditionally does not get counterspells.

Personally, I think Brazen Bluff is a fantastic Commander card. It's versatile and creates all sorts of different scenarios and opportunities for social interaction.

What do you think of the Star Trek release so far? Whether you're a trekkie or not, I'm keen to hear people's thoughts over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: D&D's new World of Warcraft book faces delays - in other news, water is wet
content:
Dungeons and Dragons publisher Wizards of the Coast has announced yet another shipping delay. D&D World of Warcraft is expected to reach North American stores after the book's early access release date on November 3. According to a D&DBeyond post, "an unforeseen delay in shipment" is to blame, and products are expected to be widely available "on or around global release on November 17".

Wizards of the Coast stresses these delays mainly impact the D&D World of Warcraft miniatures, but the rulebook itself, plus related map packs and DM screens, may be affected. "Exact delay timing will vary locally, but D&D: World of Warcraft Gameplay Expansion books and the Murloc Mini may arrive a few days after the Early Access date of November 3, though many will receive these items on time", it says.

"We know this is frustrating for those who were excited to get these books to their D&D table on Early Access release day, and we get that", Wizards' post adds. "We're working with our distribution partners to get product to stores as quickly as possible."

Longtime followers of the tabletop RPG will be disappointed by this news, but it's hardly surprising. Almost every official 5.5e book has been plagued by manufacturing or shipping issues.

Ravenloft: The Horrors Within was delayed in Europe due to shipping and logistics issues. Eberron: Forge of the Artificer was delayed worldwide due to manufacturing defects. The Forgotten Realms books, similarly, were delayed in Europe and Asia, while copies of the new DM's guide saw shipping delays in the Asia Pacific region.

Arcana Unleashed's ultimate bundle was delayed due to a truck accident. Dragon Delves was delayed in Europe and the UK due to shipping challenges, and even alternate cover copies of the Player's Handbook saw delivery delays outside the US.

This isn't a problem exclusive to tabletop RPGs, either. Wizards of the Coast's other tabletop darling, Magic: The Gathering, saw four sets in a row delayed this recently. Hasbro CFO Gina Goetter said in a recent Hasbro investor call that "we are producing more [MTG] product than at any point in history", and you have to wonder what impact that has on actually getting product to customers.

However much paper Wizards prints, though, external factors are more likely behind these constant delays. International shipping has faced stormy seas in recent years. Sometimes, those rough waters are literal - climate change is just one of many factors impacting global shipping.

Other times, they're more metaphorical. Political tension, war, tariff instability, and disruption in major locations like the Red Sea, the Suez Canal, and the Strait of Hormuz all contribute to an increasingly unstable shipping climate. Wizards of the Coast may be having shipping problems, but it's far from alone.

Want to keep up with the latest Dungeons and Dragons news? We share stories and discussions daily in the Wargamer Discord. Or, if you'd like to focus less on shipping and more on playing, our guides to DnD classes and DnD races can help.

title: Three new Pokémon trademarks hint at legendary beast triple set
content:
On October 21, 2026, Creatures Inc filed three new trademarks with the Japan Patent Office, which appear to be for upcoming Pokémon TCG sets or products. With the names Magma Pulse, Lightning Impact, and Aurora Ripples, each one corresponds to a particular Pokémon type, and this likely lines up with Entei, Raikou, and Suicune, the three Legendary Beasts from Johto.

After all, we already know these legendary Pokémon are at the center of the 'ex star' launch coming next year, thanks to the trailer that was shown at Worlds. However, what we do not know is what 'ex star' actually is. It's described as a series on the official Pokémon YouTube channel, but - as many fans have pointed out - it seems very strange to have a brand new series between Mega Evolution and the launch of Winds and Waves next year.

It seems possible that this could be Pokémon's very first triple set, a linked release with different groups of cards available in each pack. While this would be new for the physical TCG, it has worked before on Pokémon Pocket, and The Pokémon Company did quite recently release the first double set for English audiences with Black Bolt and White Flare.

There was actually a fourth trademark filed at the same time, for 'Battle Start Deck', though we don't know if this is linked in any way to the other three. If this is connected to the Legendary Beast products, then perhaps it is the return of half-decks, 30 card decks that support an extremely fast-paced format. These haven't been seen since the XY era, but in 2009, they were called 'Battle Starter decks'. You could have one for Suicune, one for Entei, and one for Raikou.

On the other hand, perhaps looking back that far is a reach. And perhaps whatever's going on with the ex star series and the legendary beasts has nothing to do with this new deck type.

It remains a confusing mystery, but you can help us get to the bottom of it by sharing your views with us.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.
